name: Mathi-Muktheeswarar Temple, Sethalapathy (Tiruthiladaipathi)
deity: Shiva as Mathi-Muktheeswarar (Muktheeswarar, the lord of liberation), with the goddess Porkodi Nayaki (Swarnavalli, Maragathavalli)
period: Tevaram era (hymned 7th century); later Chola structural temple
summary: Sethalapathy, the Tevaram's Tiruthiladaipathi, near Poonthottam in the Kaveri delta, honours Shiva as Mathi-Muktheeswarar — the lord of liberation, mukti — with the goddess Porkodi Nayaki, also called Swarnavalli. A Paadal Petra Sthalam hymned by Tirugnana Sambandar, it is a small shrine on the southern bank of the Kaveri whose very name carries the promise of release.

sections.history: Sethalapathy, the Tiruthiladaipathi of the Tevaram hymns, lies near Poonthottam, about 25 km from Mayiladuthurai, in Tiruvarur district on the southern bank of the Kaveri (older listings place it in Nagapattinam). It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, hymned by Tirugnana Sambandar in the second Thirumurai. The stone temple is of the Chola period and later, standing over a site held sacred since the age of the Tevaram saints; by local account the temple received land from a king remembered in its history.
sections.architecture: A Dravidian delta shrine of modest scale, the temple enshrines Mathi-Muktheeswarar — Muktheeswarar, the lord of liberation — in the sanctum, with the goddess Porkodi Nayaki, also called Swarnavalli and Maragathavalli, in her own shrine, a Nandi and the parivara devatas. The temple keeps the simple, well-ordered plan of the smaller Kaveri-bank sanctuaries.
sections.legends: The lord's name Muktheeswarar — 'the lord of mukti, of release' — carries the central promise of the place: that worship here grants liberation. The goddess's names, Porkodi Nayaki and Swarnavalli, both mean 'the golden creeper,' a graceful image of Devi. The sthala tradition, like that of many smaller delta shrines, is preserved chiefly in local memory and the verses of Sambandar, and the village name is linked to the offering of tila (sesame) in the ancestral rites that the delta's rivers invite.
sections.festivals: The temple observes Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March), Navaratri in Purattasi (September–October) and the Mondays of Karthikai, with Pradosha worship, at the quiet scale of a village shrine. Pilgrims on the Paadal Petra trail of the southern Kaveri include Sethalapathy among their stops.
sections.experience: At Sethalapathy the pilgrim comes to a small shrine whose name itself speaks of liberation. Before Mathi-Muktheeswarar and the golden-creeper goddess Porkodi Nayaki, the visitor finds the unhurried grace of a delta sanctuary that has kept the Tevaram's promise of mukti alive on the southern bank of the Kaveri.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Sethalapathy is near Poonthottam, about 3 km away, on the Tiruvarur–Mayiladuthurai road, roughly 25 km from Mayiladuthurai (PIN 609503). Mayiladuthurai and Tiruvarur are the nearest rail heads, with buses via Poonthottam and local taxis to the village.
